idiom_name: abstract Expr base + concrete node classes with named members
implementation_notes: The classic C++ realization is an abstract base with a virtual destructor and one concrete class per node kind that owns its named children (std::unique_ptr<Expr> left, right), with node-specific operations as virtual member functions and traversal as overrides. The type system enforces each concrete node's field set, so this form stays justified whenever nodes carry behaviour or the codebase already uses runtime polymorphism; the C-style tag-and-cast structure is unnecessary here.
pitfalls: Storing children by value slices the derived part; children must be pointers or references, and the base needs a virtual destructor.
std::unique_ptr members make nodes move-only: copying a tree requires an explicit clone operation, and a missing one shows up only when a pass tries to copy a node.
Every visited node costs one or more virtual calls; irrelevant for compilers that walk a tree a handful of times, measurable in tight repeated passes.

variants.name: std::variant node alternatives with named fields
variants.implementation_notes: From C++17 the same tree can be modelled as a variant over small structs whose members are the named children (struct Binary { Expr left; Op op; Expr right; }), with recursion supplied by std::unique_ptr or a wrapper, and each pass written as a std::visit over an overload set. Choose it when the AST is mostly data and passes are free functions; the virtual class hierarchy remains better when nodes need stateful behaviour, protected invariants or non-virtual interfaces.
pitfalls: A recursive variant must indirect through a pointer (or a recursive wrapper): a variant that contains itself by value does not compile.
std::visit needs an exhaustive overload set; a generic fallback lambda silently swallows newly added alternatives, so keep the overload set closed and let the compiler reject unknown alternatives.
